titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §100–111: the merchant, his agent and the tavern-keeper (xvii 1 – xviii 49)
part: Laws §100–111 · the merchant, his agent & the tavern-keeper (Col. xvii 1 – xviii 49)
about: Twelve laws on the trader’s two helpers: the merchant’s agent, who carries his silver and goods out on the road, and the tavern-keeper, who sells beer on credit. The first of them, the end of the law on the agent’s account, is the first thing the stele gives again after the erased columns (the beginning of that law was read from the Nippur tablet in the part before): the agent writes out the interest on the silver he took and pays his merchant (§100); if he found no profit he doubles it (§101), if he met a loss he returns the capital (§102), and if an enemy robs him on the road he swears an oath and goes free (§103). When goods are handed over for trading the agent must take a sealed receipt for what he gives back, and silver without one is not entered in the account (§104–105). An agent who takes silver and then disowns his merchant pays three times over; a merchant who disowns his agent pays six times (§106–107). The tavern-keeper laws follow: grain refused and silver taken by the heavy weight, and the beer-rate cut below the grain-rate, is punished by drowning (§108); criminals gathering in her house and not brought to the palace, by death (§109); a priestess of the cloister who opens or enters a tavern is burned (§110); beer lent on credit is repaid in grain at harvest (§111). Signs: where a Sumerogram is a group, Harper’s glossary gave its signs and the plates were matched to them; the notes say where that rests on his word.

sentences.l: The-interest of-the-silver as-much-as he-took he-shall-write-out-and, his-days they-shall-count-and, his-merchant he-shall-pay.
sentences.i: The interest on the silver, as much as he took, he shall write out; and they shall count his days, and he shall pay his merchant.
sentences.n: This is the end of a law whose beginning stood in the erased columns (the previous part gives it from the Nippur tablet: a merchant gives silver to his agent to trade with and sends him on a journey). The stele picks it up in the middle, so the subject, the agent, is not written here. What you need to read it: ṣibāt kaspim, “the interest of the silver” (ṣibtum), with mala ilqû, “as much as he took” — mala, “as much as”, starts a relative clause and its verb ends in the subjunctive -u. isaddarma is the verb sadārum, “to set in a row, put in order”, so “to write out (an account)”; Harper lists the same forms under šaṭāru, “to write”, and the sense is the same. imannûma is manûm, “to count”, in the 3rd person plural: an impersonal “they shall count”, as we would say “his days shall be counted” — probably the days the silver was out, since interest runs by the day. Last, the merchant is paid: tamkāršu ippal, “he shall pay his merchant” (apālum, “to answer, pay”). Each -ma joins one step of the reckoning to the next (the “and” chain). ūmīšu is written UD-mi-šu: the day-sign UD, a phonetic -mi and -šu, “his”.

sentences.l: If where he-went profit not he-saw, the-silver he-took he-shall-double-and, the-agent to-the-merchant shall-give.
sentences.i: If, where he went, he saw no profit, he shall double the silver he took, and the agent shall give it to the merchant.
sentences.n: The agent is the šamallûm, the merchant’s travelling trader. His name is a Sumerogram, three signs that Harper’s glossary gives as SA.GAN.LAL (the modern ŠAMAN₂.LÁ): I wrote them ŠÀ.GAN₂.LÁ and they recur all through the part; the first two signs are the uncertain ones on the plate. A šumma-clause with ašar, “where”: ašar illiku, “where he went” (the verb takes -u after ašar), then nēmelam lā ītamar, “he did not see profit”; in a šumma-clause the negative is lā (the main-clause “shall not” is ul, as in §105). kaspam ilqû is a relative clause with no ša: “the silver (that) he took”. uštašannâma is uncertain: šanûm is “to repeat, do twice”, and this Š-stem perfect is read “he shall double (it)”, which fits the penalty; the same word occurs in earlier parts of the code. The ruling ends with ana tamkārim inaddin, “to the merchant he shall give”: inaddin is the present of nadānum, “to give”, used for “shall”.

sentences.l: If a-merchant to an-agent silver for a-kindness he-has-given-and,
sentences.i: If a merchant has given silver to an agent as a favour, and
sentences.n: The law goes on in the next unit: this is only the first half of its “if” (the -ma at the end of ittadinma, “he has given, and”, hands the sentence on). The new word is tadmiqtum, Harper’s tadmiktu, “favor”: it comes from damāqum, “to be good”, and means “a doing of good, a kindness”. Silver given ana tadmiqtim, “for a kindness”, looks like an advance made on trust, but the commercial sense is a guess from the words. ittadin is the perfect of nadānum, “to give”, the tense for something already done (the present inaddin of §101 is “he shall give”). kaspam is the usual KÙ.BABBAR, with no ending written.

sentences.l: where he-went a-loss he-saw, the-capital of-the-silver to-the-merchant he-shall-return.
sentences.i: and where he went he met a loss, he shall give the merchant back the capital of the silver.
sentences.n: The rest of §102. The two halves of §101 and §102 mirror each other: there “he saw no profit” (nēmelam lā ītamar), here “he saw a loss” (bitiqtam ītamar), the verb amārum, “to see”, meaning “to meet with”. bitiqtum is “loss, damage” (Harper bitiktu). The ruling is that he returns only the capital: qaqqad kaspim, “the head of the silver”, is the principal as against the interest — the stele spells it ga-ga-ad, with g, for the word the code elsewhere writes SAG.DU. utâr is the present of târum in the D-stem, “he shall hand back”.

sentences.l: If on-the-road in his-going an-enemy whatever that he-carried has-made-him-throw-down, the-agent the-oath of-the-god shall-swear-and shall-go-free.
sentences.i: If, on the road as he was going, an enemy has made him throw down whatever he was carrying, the agent shall swear the oath of the god and go free.
sentences.n: A robbery on the road, and the agent is cleared by an oath. ḫarrānam ina alākišu, “on the road, in his going”: ḫarrānam is the road as an adverb (accusative), and alākišu, “his going”, is the infinitive of alākum with -šu. mimma ša našû is “anything that he carried” (našûm, “to carry”, with the relative -u). uštaddišu is the Š-stem of nadûm, “to throw”, plus “him”: the enemy “made him throw (it) down”, that is, took it from him by force. nīš ilim izakkarma is the oath formula: nīšum, “raising (of the hand)”, so “the oath of the god”, with zakārum, “to name, declare”: he “declares” the oath. ūtaššar is the D-stem of wašārum, “to let go”, in the passive sense: “he shall be released”, Harper’s “to go free”.

sentences.l: If a-merchant to an-agent grain wool oil and any goods for trading he-gave,
sentences.i: If a merchant gave an agent grain, wool, oil, or any other goods to trade with,
sentences.n: The “if” of §104, which runs on into the next unit. This is a list: three Sumerograms in a row — ŠE, grain (šeʾam); SIG, wool (šipâtam), and Ì.GIŠ, oil (šamnam) — and then u mimma bīšam, “and any goods”. For the list I follow Harper’s glossary for the signs: the wool sign is given there as SIG, and the plate sign (a box with a long wedge) is matched to it by his entry, not by shape; the oil is NI plus GIŠ, which Harper’s list shows as the pair for šamnu. ana pašārim is ana with an infinitive, “for trading”; Harper’s glossary gives pašāru as “to trade”, so the word was only a guess in the Nippur part and is sure here. The merchant’s act is the preterite iddin, “he gave”, here a plain past (the perfect ittadin in §102 gave “has given”).

sentences.l: The-agent the-silver shall-write-out-and to-the-merchant shall-return; the-agent a-sealed-receipt of-the-silver which to-the-merchant he-gives shall-take.
sentences.i: The agent shall write out the silver and give it back to the merchant; the agent shall take a sealed receipt for the silver that he gives to the merchant.
sentences.n: The ruling of §104, in two halves: first the agent reckons up the silver (isaddarma, as in §100) and returns it (utâr), then he takes a kanīk kaspim, “a sealed receipt for silver”. kanīkum, Harper’s “sealed receipt”, is a clay tablet that bears the seal (kanākum, “to seal”) — the receipt the merchant gives back; it is not the same word as kunukkum, “seal”. ša ana tamkārim inaddinu is a relative clause: “which he gives to the merchant”. ileqqi is the present of leqûm, “to take”. The point of the receipt comes in §105: without it the silver does not count.

sentences.l: If the-agent was-careless-and the-sealed-receipt of-silver which to-the-merchant he-gave not he-took,
sentences.i: If the agent was careless and did not take a sealed receipt for the silver that he gave to the merchant,
sentences.n: The case the previous law guards against. itēgima is the perfect of egûm, “to be careless, neglect” (Harper: “to be careless”), with -ma, “and”. The negative: lā ilteqe, “he did not take” — in a šumma-clause the verb is negated with lā, while the ruling that follows says ul (ul iššakkan, next unit). ilteqe is the perfect of leqûm, “he has taken”, from the same verb as ileqqi, “he shall take”, in §104. The sentence continues in the next unit.

sentences.l: silver without-sealed-receipt to-the-account not shall-be-put.
sentences.i: Silver without a sealed receipt shall not be entered in the account.
sentences.n: The ruling. kaspi lā kanīkim is “silver of-no sealed receipt”, that is, “silver without a sealed receipt”: lā before a noun in the genitive means “without”. The account is nikkazzum, Harper’s “account, credit” (modern editions normalise it nikkassum, “account, reckoning”); the spelling ni-ik-ka-az-zi-im, with the sign AZ, is the reason for Harper’s z, and the exact sense, “account” or “credit”, is not certain. ul iššakkan is the N-stem (passive) present of šakānum, “to put”: “it shall not be put”. ul + present is a flat prohibition, the way a ruling is usually phrased in the code.

sentences.l: If an-agent silver from a-merchant took-and, his-merchant he-denied,
sentences.i: If an agent took silver from a merchant and then disowned his merchant,
sentences.n: ilqēma is leqûm in the perfect, “he took”, plus -ma. Then the agent turns on his merchant: tamkāršu ittakir, “he disowned his merchant”. nakārum is “to be hostile, to dispute, to deny” (Harper: “to dispute”): with an accusative object, “he denied his merchant”, that is, refused to acknowledge the debt. The -šu on tamkāršu is “his” (a noun), not an object suffix on the verb: the agent is the one who acts, and the merchant who is acted on. The ruling comes in the next unit, in which the merchant proves the agent’s guilt. ittakir is the perfect (Harper I,2: “he has denied”), the tense of a finished deed.

sentences.l: That merchant before the-god and witnesses, in the-taking of-the-silver, the-agent shall-convict-and; the-agent the-silver as-much-as he-took, three-fold to-the-merchant shall-give.
sentences.i: That merchant shall convict the agent, before the god and witnesses, of taking the silver, and the agent shall give the merchant three times as much as he took.
sentences.n: The merchant brings proof; the agent pays threefold. tamkārum šū is “that merchant” (šū, “he, that”, set after the noun). ina maḫar ilim u šībī, “before the god and the witnesses” (maḫar, “in the presence of”; šībī, genitive plural of šībum, “witness”). ina kaspim leqîm is ina with the infinitive of leqûm: “in the taking of the silver”, that is, “for having taken it”. ukānma is the D-stem of kânum, “to establish; to convict”, the verb of proof: ukān šamallâm, “he shall convict the agent”. a-du 3-šu is the code’s multiplier: adi, “up to”, with a numeral and -šu, “up to threefold”, that is “three times (as much)”. Harper’s a-du is a variant spelling of adi, and the plate has the sign DU, so it is said adu. Harper’s tamka-rum, split by the page turn, is the single Sumerogram DAM.GÀR; the line-end hyphens in šamal-lûm and kas-pam are Harper’s typesetting.

sentences.l: If a-merchant the-agent entrusted-and, the-agent whatever that the-merchant gave-him to his-merchant has-returned,
sentences.i: If a merchant has entrusted an agent (with goods), and the agent has returned to his merchant everything that the merchant gave him,
sentences.n: Now the other way round: the agent is honest. iqīpma is the verb qiāpum, “to entrust” (Harper’s “to intrust”, in his glossary under kapu): the merchant “entrusted the agent”, here with goods, though the goods are not named. mimma ša tamkārum iddinušum, “everything that the merchant gave him” — a relative clause whose verb has the subjunctive -u and the dative -šum, “to him”. uttēr is the perfect of târum in the D-stem, “he has given back” (Harper’s ut-te-ir): the same verb as utâr in §102. The “if” continues in the next unit. Harper’s line division puts ana tamkāršu, “to his merchant”, at the end of XVII 72 and uttēr alone on XVIII 1; the stele has both lines.

sentences.l: the-merchant whatever that the-agent gave-him has-denied-him,
sentences.i: and the merchant has denied having received whatever the agent gave him,
sentences.n: The wrong. tamkārum mimma ša šamallûm iddinušum ittakiršu: the thing at issue is put first, “everything that the agent gave him”, and the verb follows, “the merchant denied him” — ittakir-šu with -šu as an object, “him”, the agent. So the merchant disowns the agent over what he handed over, which I take to mean that he denies having received it; the grammar says only “he denied him”. It is the same verb nakārum as in §106, where the agent was the one who denied. The sentence is still a protasis; the ruling follows in the next unit.

sentences.l: That agent before the-god and witnesses the-merchant shall-convict-and; the-merchant because-of his-agent he-denied, whatever that he-took, six-fold to-the-agent shall-give.
sentences.i: That agent shall convict the merchant before the god and witnesses, and because the merchant denied his agent he shall give the agent six times whatever he took.
sentences.n: The ruling, the mirror of §106: now the agent proves his case, and the merchant pays sixfold, twice the agent’s penalty. The wording repeats §106, the roles swapped: ina maḫar ilim u šībī … ukānma, a-du 6-šu … inaddin. The new words: aššum, “because (of)”, followed by the clause tamkārum aššum šamallîšu ikkiru, “the merchant, because he denied his agent” — ikkiru is the preterite of nakārum with the subjunctive -u that every verb takes after aššum. šamallīšu is the Sumerogram ŠÀ.GAN₂.LÁ with -šu, “his”. mimma ša ilqû is “whatever he took”: here the subject of ilqû is the merchant, who took the agent’s returned goods. Harper’s ša-mallî-šu, split at the line end, is one word.

sentences.l: If a-tavern-keeper for the-price of-beer grain not she-received, by-the-large stone silver she-received,
sentences.i: If a tavern-keeper did not accept grain as the price of beer, but took silver by the heavy weight,
sentences.n: The tavern-keeper laws begin (§108–111); the tavern-keeper is the woman who brews and sells beer and wine. Her name is the Sumerogram ŠAL.GEŠ.TIN.NA, “woman” + “wine”: Harper gives only the signs, and I read it sābītum (“tavern-keeper”) as the modern editors do. Its signs, from Harper’s list, are SAL, GEŠ (his sign 94, the one the code also uses for “beer” and for syllable bi), TIN (no. 178) and NA. The first rule of the trade is the standard of payment: ana šīm šikarim šeʾam lā imtaḫar, “for the price of beer she did not accept grain” — šīm, “the price”, is the sign ŠÁM (Harper’s no. 83, šîmu); šikarim, “of beer”, is KAŠ (the sign 94 again; Harper’s šikaru). imtaḫar is the perfect of maḫārum, “to receive” (Harper: “to receive”; the same verb meant “to face” in the other parts). ina abnim rabîtim is “by the large stone”: NA₄ (Harper’s abnu) is the stone used as a weight, so a heavy standard — she takes silver weighed on a heavier standard than the usual one (the sense is from the context). rabîtim is the feminine of rabûm, “great”, with the stone treated as feminine.

sentences.l: and the-rate of-beer to the-rate of-grain she-has-made-small, that tavern-keeper they-shall-convict-her-and, into-the-water they-shall-throw-her.
sentences.i: and has made the rate of beer less than the rate of grain, they shall convict that tavern-keeper and throw her into the water.
sentences.n: Second fraud, then the penalty: she drowned. u maḫīr šikarim ana maḫīr šeʾim umtaṭṭi, “and she has made the rate of beer small against the rate of grain”: maḫīrum, “market rate, price” (written KI.LAM, which Harper reads maḫiru), and umtaṭṭi, the D-stem perfect of maṭûm, “to be small”, “she has lessened”. The penalty: ukannūšima, “they shall convict her, and” (kânum, D-stem, the verb of proof, with the feminine -ši, “her”), then ana mê inaddûši, “they shall throw her into the water” — nadûm, “to throw”, and mû, “water”: the penalty is death by drowning, and the verb is the same one the code uses for casting a body into the river. In inaddûši the stone is damaged on the middle sign: Harper prints i-na-[ad]-du-u-ši with the AD in brackets, so that sign is his restoration; the word is certain from the sense. The verbs are in the plural with no subject: “they” are the judges.

sentences.l: If a-tavern-keeper criminals in her-house have-gathered-and, those criminals not she-seized-and
sentences.i: If criminals have gathered in a tavern-keeper’s house, and she did not seize those criminals
sentences.n: Tavern as a place where rogues meet. ṣarrūtum is Harper’s “outlaws, rowdies, traitors”: criminals or rebels, a plural noun, not a title. ittarkasūma is the N-stem perfect of rakāsum, “to bind”, so “they have bound themselves together, gathered, conspired” (Harper’s “collect”). bītiša is bītum, “house” (the sign É) with -ša, “her”. ṣarrūtim šunūti, “those criminals” (šunūti is “them”, masculine plural). iṣṣabtamma is the perfect of ṣabātum, “to seize”, with the ventive -am (“to here”) and -ma: lā iṣṣabtamma, “and she did not seize”. The sentence goes on in the next unit.

sentences.l: to the-palace not she-led, that tavern-keeper shall-be-killed.
sentences.i: and did not bring them to the palace, that tavern-keeper shall be killed.
sentences.n: The ruling is death. ana ekallim lā irdiam, “she did not lead (them) to the palace”: ekallum, the palace (É.GAL, “great house”), the king’s court; irdiam is from redûm, “to drive, lead, bring” (Harper’s “to conduct”), with the ventive -am, “here”. The tavern-keeper is the one who has failed in a duty: it is her business to hand criminals over. ŠAL.GEŠ.TIN.NA šī, “that (she) tavern-keeper”, uses the feminine pronoun šī; the penalty is iddâk, the N-stem of dâkum, “to kill”: “she shall be killed”, the code’s ordinary death sentence, and the same word as for a man.

sentences.l: If a-priestess who in-the-cloister not she-dwells,
sentences.i: If a priestess who does not live in the cloister
sentences.n: The “if” of §110 begins with two uncertain items. The first word is three signs, ŠAL.NIN.AN: Harper’s transliteration prints aššatum NIN.AN, “a woman, a NIN.AN”, and his index lists the group as SAL.NIN.AN; he does not read it as a word, but I take it as one, nadītum, the cloistered priestess of the code (the same reading the earlier part records for the lone SAL at §40: Harper “wife”, modern editions nadītum). The reading is uncertain: it rests on the sign group and the context, not on a spelled word. The second is MAL.GE.A: Harper leaves it unread; I take it as gagûm, the cloister, the walled house in which these priestesses lived, so ša ina gagîm lā wašbat is “who does not live in the cloister” (wašbat is the stative of wašābum, “to live”). The cloister reading is also uncertain.

sentences.l: a-wine-house she-has-opened, or for beer to a-wine-house she-has-entered, that woman they-shall-burn-her.
sentences.i: opens a tavern, or goes into a tavern for beer, they shall burn that woman.
sentences.n: The offence and the penalty: she is burned. bīt karānim is “wine-house”, the Sumerogram É followed by GEŠ.TIN.NA, which Harper reads karânu, “wine” (the sign list gives karânu for the group): the tavern, the same trade as the sābītum’s. iptete is the perfect of petûm, “to open”: “she has opened (one)”; iterub is the perfect of erēbum, “to enter” (Harper’s “to enter”). u lū is “or”. The penalty: awīltam šuāti iqallûši, “that woman they shall burn her” — awīltum, “woman, lady”, the feminine of awīlum, put first for emphasis and then taken up by -ši, “her”; iqallûši is the present of qalûm, “to burn” (Harper’s kalû, with his k), plural, again with an unnamed “they”. The code says only “burn”; it does not say whether she is alive.

sentences.l: If a-tavern-keeper sixty qa of-beer, U.SA.KA.NI, on-credit she-gave, at-the-harvest fifty qa of-grain she-shall-take.
sentences.i: If a tavern-keeper gave sixty qa of U.SA.KA.NI beer on credit, at harvest she shall take fifty qa of grain.
sentences.n: The last law of the part: beer lent against the harvest. The qa is the measure of capacity (about a litre); Harper writes “LX QA” and “L QA”. On the plate the sixty is the single vertical wedge and I could not make out a separate sign for qa after it; the fifty is a single ligature, the numeral and the measure fused (the sign Unicode calls 5 BAN₂, “five times ten qa”, and Harper’s list of numerals shows “50 KA” in the same way), so “sixty qa” and “fifty qa” are my reading of Harper’s expansion. U.SA.KA.NI is four signs that Harper leaves unread; it must name a kind of beer, but I do not know the word, so it is said usakani and not translated. The shape of line 49 is not certain either: I could not match every sign cluster of the plate with the words. a-na di-ib-tim is ana dibtim, “on credit (?)” — Harper’s own glossary has diptu, “credit(?)”, with a question mark. ina ebūrim, “at harvest” (BURU₁₄, as in §47). The law fixes the repayment: grain, at the harvest, and fifty qa for the sixty of beer.
